title: Evals: online monitoring, drift and red-teaming
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Traces, cost and latency arithmetic, percentiles, sampled online judging, drift types, canary and shadow releases, and red-team regression suites for LLM applications.
source: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions; Google SRE book (error budgets); OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications; Langfuse docs; garak, PyRIT, promptfoo docs

questions.prompt: Hypothetical prices: input tokens cost $2 per million and output tokens cost $8 per million. A request uses 1500 input tokens and 250 output tokens. What does 10,000 such requests cost, in dollars?
questions.explanation: Per request: 1500 x $2/1M = $0.003 and 250 x $8/1M = $0.002, total $0.005. Times 10,000 gives $50. Output tokens are priced higher, so verbose answers and retry loops show up quickly in cost dashboards.

questions.prompt: Over a window of 200 requests the p95 latency is 4.2 seconds. About how many of those 200 requests were slower than 4.2 seconds?
questions.explanation: p95 means 95% of requests are at or below the value, so 5% of 200 = 10 are slower. Averages hide exactly these tail requests.

questions.prompt: You receive 40,000 traces a day and an LLM judge scores a random 5% sample at $0.002 per judged trace. What is the daily judge cost in dollars?
questions.explanation: 5% of 40,000 = 2,000 judged traces; 2,000 x $0.002 = $4. Sampling keeps online quality monitoring cheap while still showing trends.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: For an LLM endpoint you should alert on p95 or p99 latency, not only the mean.
questions.reason: The mean hides the slowest requests, which can affect a noticeable fraction of users.

whys.a: Correct: tail percentiles expose slow outliers (long generations, retries, cold caches) that a mean smooths away.
whys.b: R is the direct reason, not a side fact.
whys.d: A is true; SRE practice monitors percentiles.

questions.explanation: Track time to first token as well as total time for streaming responses.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Each LLM span in a trace should record the model name, version and token counts.
questions.reason: Token counts alone fully determine the latency of a request.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, not merely unrelated.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because cost and regressions are attributed per model and prompt version, but latency also depends on queueing, network, tool calls and output length.
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Add prompt version, retrieval index version and user/session ids (hashed) as span attributes.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Output quality can degrade even when you have shipped no code change.
questions.reason: Provider-side model updates and shifts in the distribution of user inputs can change behaviour.

whys.a: Correct: both are real causes of drift with no deploy on your side, which is why you pin versions and monitor continuously.
whys.b: R is the mechanism, so it does explain A.

questions.explanation: Pin model snapshots, run the golden suite on a schedule, and watch online scores.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Scoring a random sample of production traces with an LLM judge keeps the cost of online evaluation bounded.
questions.reason: Thumbs-down feedback from users is a useful signal for choosing which traces to review.

whys.a: R is true but it is about selecting traces, not about bounding cost.
whys.b: Correct: sampling bounds spend (A) and feedback-driven selection (R) is true but a different idea.

questions.explanation: Combine random sampling for trend lines with targeted sampling of low-rated or high-cost traces.

questions.prompt: Match each monitoring tool or practice to its purpose.

right.text: Follows one request through retrieval, LLM and tool calls with timings
Pages on-call when p95 latency crosses a threshold
Scores a sample of live outputs for quality
Replays injection, jailbreak and data-leak prompts before release
Mirrors live traffic to a new version without affecting users

questions.explanation: A good answer pairs each signal (traces, metrics, evals) with the question it answers (where, how bad, how good).

questions.prompt: In Python with OpenTelemetry, write a function call_llm(prompt) that runs inside a span named "llm.call" (use a tracer from trace.get_tracer) and sets a span attribute "llm.model" to MODEL before calling client.generate(prompt).
questions.starter:
from opentelemetry import trace
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

checks.label: opens the span as a context manager

questions.explanation: start_as_current_span ends the span and records exceptions for you. A decorator or start_span with try/finally also works but is more verbose; this check expects the context-manager form. The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions standardise attribute names such as gen_ai.request.model (still in development), so prefer those over invented keys like llm.model in real code.

questions.prompt: ATTACKS is a list of prompt-injection strings and SECRET is the system-prompt secret. Write a parametrized pytest test_no_leak that calls chatbot(prompt) and asserts SECRET never appears in the reply.
questions.explanation: Red-team prompts become regression tests: every new jailbreak you find is appended to ATTACKS. Also test paraphrased or encoded leaks, since exact-string checks miss base64 or translated output.

questions.prompt: Cost per request doubled overnight with no deploy. What do you check first?

options.text: Per-trace token counts and retries, then provider changes.
options.why: Right: traces reveal prompt growth, retry loops or a changed model, all causes of a cost jump.

options.text: Whether the primary database needs another index on the users table to speed up login queries.
options.why: Database indexes do not drive LLM token spend.

options.text: Whether the CDN cache hit ratio for static images dropped during the last twenty four hours.
options.why: Static assets are unrelated to LLM billing.

options.text: Whether unit tests still pass on the main branch after the last merge.
options.why: Passing tests say nothing about live token usage.

questions.explanation: Slice cost by model, prompt version, tenant and endpoint. Budgets and per-tenant limits turn a surprise into an alert.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a red-team suite for an LLM assistant that reads documents and calls tools? Select all that apply.

options.text: Indirect prompt injection hidden inside retrieved documents.
options.why: Right: untrusted content that reaches the model is a primary attack path.

options.text: Jailbreak attempts that try to override the system prompt.
Attempts to extract secrets, PII or other tenants' data.
options.why: Right: data exfiltration is a core risk.
Happy paths belong in the golden set; red-teaming needs adversarial inputs.

questions.explanation: Tools such as garak, PyRIT and promptfoo automate attack generation; the OWASP LLM Top 10 is a good checklist.

questions.text: {1} drift is a change in the distribution of inputs, {2} drift is a change in what the correct output is for the same input, and pinning a model {3} avoids silent provider upgrades.
questions.explanation: A moving alias such as "latest" can change behaviour with no deploy. Pin a dated snapshot and upgrade deliberately after running the golden suite.

questions.prompt: True or false: it is always fine to store raw user prompts and model outputs in traces indefinitely, because it helps debugging.

options.why: Debugging value does not override privacy and retention duties.
Correct: prompts can contain PII or secrets, so redact or hash sensitive fields, set retention limits and restrict access.

questions.explanation: Consider sampling full payloads and keeping only metadata for the rest.

questions.prompt: Your LLM endpoint has a 99.5% success-rate SLO and serves 200,000 requests a day. How many failed requests per day exhaust the error budget?
questions.explanation: The budget is 0.5% of 200,000 = 1,000 failures. Treat provider timeouts, refusals you count as failures and guardrail blocks consistently when defining a 'success'.
